info.buildingYear: The year of construction reveals the typical insulation standard and helps estimate the energy demand.
info.windowAge: Older windows often have higher heat losses – the age helps with the assessment.
info.ventilation: HRV stands for heat recovery: the ventilation uses the warmth of the exhaust air to pre-heat fresh air.
info.insulation: A rough self-assessment is enough – you don't need to measure anything precisely.
info.goals: Your goals help the app prioritise the right measurements and tips.
info.occupancy: As an owner, larger measures are often possible than when renting.
info.persons: The number of people significantly affects hot water and electricity use.
info.livingArea: The heated living area is a key figure for the heating demand.
info.heatGenerators: Multiple selection is possible if several systems heat in parallel.
info.hotWater: Is the hot water produced by the heating system or by a separate device?
info.pv: A PV system supplies your own electricity and changes the energy balance.
info.fireplace: An additional fireplace/stove adds room heat and should be recorded.
info.instruments: This overview is information, not a question – the app derives it from what its checks actually require. There is nothing to select here.
info.smartHome: Smart devices can provide consumption data and improve the analysis.
info.renovation: Renovations improve the insulation standard and reduce the energy demand.
info.location: Your postal code lets regional climate and weather data flow in later.
info.appliances: The fridge and freezer checks each measure a real appliance. Without this answer the app suggests checks you have nothing to measure for – and your progress would never reach 100 %. “We have none” takes the matching check out; you can undo that here at any time.

page.title: Measurements
page.subtitle: Simple, guided checks for your home.

measurements.allDone: Great – you've completed all available measurements.

byRoom.noRooms: You haven't selected any rooms yet.

common.gateHint: Answer once – it goes into your profile and can be changed there.
common.applianceChooseHint: Each appliance gets its own result.

ambient.title: Located in the {{room}}, {{temp}} °C
ambient.assumed: reference value – no room climate measurement here yet

note.cold: Below 10 °C, older thermostats no longer switch reliably – the appliance may thaw in winter even though it is cold outside. Worth checking the climate class on the rating plate.
note.moderate: A favourable spot: the cooler the surroundings, the less the appliance has to work against the heat.
note.warm: Warm surroundings – the appliance works against a larger temperature gradient and therefore runs more often. A cooler location would be the most effective change.

showerhead.title: Showerhead Test
showerhead.short: Measure your shower's water flow and uncover savings potential.

intro.videoAlt: Animation: water filling a measuring cup under a showerhead
details: Use a container of known volume – e.g. a measuring cup or bucket with a 5-litre mark.
Turn on the shower the way you normally shower (usual temperature and strength).
Hold the container fully under the stream and start the stopwatch at the same time.
Stop the time exactly when the water reaches the mark.
Tip: measure two or three times and take the average for a more accurate result.
With an instantaneous water heater: let it run briefly until the temperature is stable.

run.litersInfo: The volume of your container. Standard is 5 litres.
run.secondsInfo: The time in seconds until the container was full.

result.savingLabel: Around {{liters}} litres of hot water a year
result.sourceNote: Estimated for hot water via {{source}}. More accurate with your price set.

summary.good: Very economical – your shower head uses little water.
summary.medium: {{flow}} L/min – mid-range. A flow restrictor would still help; at this level the shower duration matters more.
summary.high: {{flow}} L/min – roughly twice that of a water-saving head. A flow restrictor brings you to about {{target}} L/min, provided your shower head has a standard thread (½ inch, the usual case).

chips.saver: Check the thread, then fit a restrictor

calculation.formula: Shower minutes per year = occupants × showers/day × minutes/shower × 365. Times the flow rate gives litres; times the temperature rise and the energy per litre and kelvin gives kWh – times your hot water source's unit price gives the cost.
calculation.flow: Flow rate of your shower head
calculation.note: Only the flow rate is measured. Shower frequency and duration are assumptions, chosen so the result lands at roughly 516 kWh per person per year – the range cited in the literature for domestic hot water is 500–600 kWh.

result.buyingNote: When buying: "eco" and "water-saving" are not protected terms – a head marketed that way can still deliver 15 L/min. What counts is the stated flow rate; below {{target}} L/min is considered economical.

fridge.title: Fridge Check
fridge.short: Check the temperature and energy use of your fridge.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring the temperature inside the fridge
steps: Put a thermometer in the fridge
details: Place the thermometer in the middle of the fridge – ideally in a glass of water, which shows the real storage temperature.
Close the door and wait several hours (overnight is best) before reading it.
Recommended: 5–7 °C in the fridge and about −18 °C in the freezer compartment.
Every degree colder than necessary noticeably increases electricity use.
While you're at it, check the door seal – if it no longer closes tightly, the appliance cools far more than needed.

run.hint: Rule of thumb: each 1 °C warmer (towards 7 °C) saves ~6% electricity. Turn the dial down and re-measure after a few hours.
run.followUpHint: Last time you were at {{temp}} °C ({{status}}). Measure again after adjusting the dial.

result.savingHint: Potential if you adjust the dial towards 7 °C (~6% per °C).

status.tooCold: Set too cold – this wastes electricity.

summary.good: The temperature is within the recommended 5–7 °C range – both efficient and safe.
summary.medium: The temperature is outside the recommended range (5–7 °C). One step on the dial is usually enough.
summary.high: The temperature is well outside the recommended range (5–7 °C): too cold wastes electricity, too warm spoils food faster.

standby.title: Standby Check
standby.short: Track down hidden power drains in standby mode.

intro.needs: You'll need a power meter (energy cost meter).
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring a TV's standby power
steps: Plug the meter between socket & device
Put device in standby, read the watts
details: For this check you need a simple plug-in power meter (energy cost meter).
Plug it between the socket and the device, put the device into standby and read the watts.
Many devices draw power around the clock even though they seem "off" – it adds up over the year.
A switchable power strip fully disconnects several devices at once.

run.duplicateHint: This device is already in the list above.

summary.good: Very efficient – barely any standby use.
summary.medium: Moderate standby use – savings potential here.
summary.high: High standby use – hidden power drains at work.

room_temperature.title: Room Climate Check
room_temperature.short: Measure room temperature and find your heating savings potential.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person measuring the room climate with a thermometer
steps: Place a thermometer in the room
details: Place the thermometer in the middle of the room at about sitting height – not right next to a radiator, window or external wall.
Wait a few minutes for the reading to stabilise before noting it.
As a guide: about 20 °C in the living room, 18 °C in the kitchen and 16–18 °C in the bedroom.
A comfortable humidity is around 40–60 %.
Every degree less saves noticeable heating energy – without becoming uncomfortable.

status.tooCold: A bit cool – every degree less saves, but mind comfort.
status.tooWarm: A bit warm – 1 °C less noticeably cuts heating costs.
status.tooDry: Rather dry – airing out or plants can help.
status.tooHumid: Rather humid – regular airing prevents mold.

draftStatus.strong: Strong draft – checking the seals pays off.

saving.title: Potential saving
saving.context: {{percent}}% less heating energy at {{delta}} °C above {{reference}} °C – proportional for this room. Rough guide value (≈6% per °C), not a forecast.

dewPoint.title: Careful when airing out
dewPoint.text: This air condenses on a basement wall at {{wall}} °C – its dew point is {{dewPoint}} °C. Mould is not caused by a percentage, but by exactly this.
dewPoint.rule: In summer, air out at night or early morning, not at midday: warm outside air brings in more moisture than it carries away.

freezer.title: Freezer Check
freezer.short: Check ice build-up and temperature to avoid wasted electricity.

intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person checking the iced-up freezer
details: Estimate the ice layer on the inner wall: from about 5 mm onwards, electricity use rises noticeably.
For the temperature, place the thermometer in the middle between the frozen items and close the door again.
Recommended is around −18 °C – colder brings hardly any benefit but costs more electricity.
Defrosting regularly saves energy and frees up space again.
Check the door seal – if it no longer closes tightly, the appliance ices up faster.

spots.title: Just a few spots
spots.hint: A few millimetres of ice in places, the rest is clear.

thin.title: Thin, all over
thin.hint: A thin layer of ice across the walls.

thick.title: Iced solid
thick.hint: Thick ice; drawers or compartments already stick.

run.noFrostHint: Great – ice-free means it runs efficiently, nothing to do.

tempStatus.tooCold: too cold – setting warmer saves power

advice.notNeeded: No defrosting needed – it is running efficiently.
advice.canWait: Defrosting can wait. Do it next time the freezer is empty anyway.
advice.worthwhile: Defrosting pays off – this layer of ice costs noticeable power.
advice.now: Defrost now. Iced up this badly, it uses far more power than needed.

result.effectEstimated: Typical for this much ice: around {{percent}} % extra consumption.

summary.medium: A few icy spots. Defrosting can wait until the freezer is empty anyway.
summary.elevated: A thin layer of ice all over – defrosting pays off, it costs noticeable power.
summary.high: Iced solid – defrost now. Like this it uses far more power than needed.

impact.title: Your savings potential
impact.info: Rough estimate: the euro savings are converted to kilowatt-hours via your electricity price and projected at about 0.38 kg CO₂ per kWh.
impact.empty: Take your first measurement to see your potential.
impact.progress: {{done}} of {{total}} measurements done – the results are listed below.

roomPicker.subtitle: Which room do you want to measure?
roomPicker.addSubtitle: A tap is enough. Size and heating can follow later in your profile.
roomPicker.emptyHint: This check needs at least one room. Add one here – it only takes a moment.

flow.planSubtitle: Recommended measurements in a sensible order.

hot_water_wait.title: Hot water wait
hot_water_wait.short: Measure how long you wait for hot water — and the potential that runs off unused.

intro.lead: Until hot water arrives, cold water often runs off unused. Find out how much.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person timing how long until hot water arrives
steps: Stop once it is clearly warm
details: Until hot water arrives, cold water often runs off unused – this check measures that wait.
Turn the tap fully to hot and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Stop as soon as the water feels clearly warm.
Measure at the tap you use most often (e.g. shower or kitchen).

run.instruction: Turn the water fully to hot, start the stopwatch — and stop as soon as it gets clearly warm.
run.stagnationHint: Measure when the pipe has cooled down – ideally in the morning before the first draw. Shortly after showering the pipe is still warm and the reading comes out too low.
run.hintStopwatch: Start the stopwatch and stop it once the water is warm.

result.explanation: In that time roughly {{liters}} L of drinking water ran off unused.
result.explanationUnknown: Drinking water ran off unused during that time – how much hasn't been measured for this tap yet.
result.reuseTitle: Collected, it can be used for

summary.good: Hot water arrives quickly – hardly any drinking water runs off unused.
summary.medium: Some drinking water runs off unused before the hot water arrives. Collected, it can still be put to use.
summary.elevated: The wait is long – a noticeable amount of drinking water runs off unused every time you draw water.
summary.high: Very long wait: a lot of drinking water is wasted per draw. Usually the cause is a long or uninsulated pipe.

calculation.formula: Wait time × flow rate = litres wasted per draw. Times draws per person per day, times occupants, times 365 gives the yearly volume; times the water price gives the cost.
calculation.note: Draws per day are a model assumption, not a measurement – calibrated for a {{persons}}-person household. The dependable figure is the volume per draw; the yearly value is an extrapolation.

furniture_spacing.title: Furniture spacing check
furniture_spacing.short: Check whether furniture or rugs are blocking your heating.

intro.lead: Unobstructed heat surfaces release their heat evenly – and the thermostat measures what it is supposed to measure. Check room by room what is in the way.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: measuring the distance between a radiator and a sofa
details: Covered heat surfaces do not lose the heat – they release it delayed and unevenly.
The cost is indirect: an enclosed thermostat reads trapped heat, shuts off too early, and the room gets turned up by hand.
Leave roughly 10 cm of air in front of radiators so air can flow in from below.
If you have a folding rule at hand, enter the distance directly – the check then derives its rating from it.
Sofas, cabinets, long curtains or casings in front of them slow heat output.
With underfloor heating, large furniture without legs and thick rugs impede output – the system then needs a higher flow temperature.
Check each room individually – often a small rearrangement already improves heat output.

questions.furniture: Is a large piece of furniture (sofa, cabinet, shelf) standing directly in front of the radiator?
questions.cover: Is the radiator covered by a casing, curtain or shelf?
questions.valve: Is the thermostatic valve enclosed by furniture, casing or a curtain?
questions.footless: Is large furniture without legs standing flat on the floor (sofa, bed, cabinet)?
questions.carpet: Is a large, thick rug lying on the heated surface?
questions.thermostat: Is the room thermostat covered by furniture, a curtain or pictures?
questions.builtin: Is the radiator built over by fitted units, a worktop or a plinth panel?
questions.towels: Are towels or laundry hanging over the radiator?

living_room.furniture: Is a sofa, armchair or sideboard standing directly in front of the radiator?

dining_room.furniture: Is a dining table, bench or cabinet standing directly in front of the radiator?

bedroom.furniture: Is the bed, a wardrobe or a chest of drawers standing directly in front of the radiator?
bedroom.footless: Is the bed or a cabinet standing without legs directly on the heated surface?

children_room.furniture: Are the bed, shelves or toy boxes standing directly in front of the radiator?

office.furniture: Is a desk, pedestal or shelf standing directly in front of the radiator?

bathroom.carpet: Is a large bath mat permanently lying on the heated surface?

kitchen.footless: Do the fitted kitchen units sit with a closed plinth on the heated surface?

run.distanceHint: Distance between the front edge of the furniture and the radiator, level with the air inlet at the bottom. At least {{target}} cm of clear space is recommended.
run.transferHint: The questions depend on it. This applies to every “{{room}}” and can be changed in your profile.
run.coverHint: A rough estimate: how much of the heated floor sits under furniture with no air gap? From about {{target}} % onwards you lose noticeable heating surface.

summary.good: Heat surface and controls work undisturbed – exactly as intended.
summary.medium: Almost everything is clear – one point slightly slows heat output.
summary.elevated: Heat is distributed unevenly – and the controls no longer work properly.
summary.high: Heat output and controls are clearly disturbed – the room needs a higher flow temperature than necessary.

result.allClear: Nothing blocks the heat surface and the temperature sensor works freely. Worth a quick check whenever you rearrange furniture.
result.mechanism: The heat is not lost – the radiator sits inside the building envelope and releases almost all of it into the room. It costs energy in three other ways: the temperature sensor reads the trapped heat, shuts off too early, the room stays cool and gets turned up by hand. On an external wall the trapped heat raises the wall temperature and with it the loss to the outside. And a higher flow temperature is needed for the same output.

valve.why: The valve controls by the temperature it measures itself. Enclosed, it reads trapped heat instead of room temperature, closes too early, the room stays cool – and gets turned up by hand. The single most relevant finding in this check.
valve.action: Let air circulate freely around the valve head. Where that is impossible, a remote sensor or a thermostat with a detached sensor helps.

cover.why: A casing, curtain or shelf slows the airflow through the radiator and shields its radiant heat. A fixed casing weighs more than a curtain because it acts permanently.
cover.action: Shorten the curtain to windowsill height, remove the shelf. A fixed casing needs openings at the bottom and top so air can flow through.

furniture.why: Furniture directly in front deflects the warm air. The heat still reaches the room, but delayed and unevenly – and on an external wall the trapped heat warms the wall too.
furniture.action: Leave roughly 10 cm of air in front of the radiator so air can flow in from below.

footless.why: Underfloor heating releases most of its heat as radiation across the open surface. Furniture without an air gap takes that area out of service – the remaining area has to compensate with a higher flow temperature.
footless.action: Choose furniture with legs or put it on glides. Even a few centimetres of air gap help.

carpet.partly: Rug on part of the surface
carpet.yes: Thick rug on the heated surface
carpet.why: A rug acts as insulation above the heat surface. The system is designed around a low thermal resistance of the floor build-up; a thick rug exceeds it and forces a higher flow temperature.
carpet.action: Use thin rugs approved for underfloor heating – marked by the symbol or by the stated thermal resistance.

thermostat.why: The room thermostat controls the entire surface. Covered, it measures the air in its hiding place rather than the room – the surface heats too long or too briefly. With slow-responding underfloor heating this hits particularly hard.
thermostat.action: Keep the thermostat clear and uncovered, not behind a curtain, furniture or a picture. Direct sunlight and draughts distort the reading too.

builtin.yes: Radiator built over by fitted units
builtin.why: In kitchens the radiator often sits behind a plinth panel or under the worktop. This is the worst case: air cannot flow in freely, trapped heat sits permanently at the valve, and it cannot be fixed by rearranging anything.
builtin.action: Fit ventilation grilles into the plinth panel and the top cover – at the bottom for intake, at the top for outlet. When replacing the kitchen, free the radiator or switch to a plinth convector with a fan.

towels.partly: Towels over the radiator now and then
towels.yes: Towels or laundry over the radiator
towels.why: Textiles over the radiator have a double effect: they shield the heat output, and their evaporative cooling keeps the valve open longer. In a bathroom the evaporated moisture also stays in the room and has to be ventilated out.
towels.action: Do not dry wet laundry on the radiator. Mount towel rails beside rather than above the radiator; ventilate thoroughly after showering.

radiator: Keep the radiator clear – place sofa/cabinet with some distance.
No casing or long curtains in front of it.
Let air circulate freely around the thermostatic valve.
underfloor: Choose furniture with legs – an air gap to the floor helps.
Avoid large, thick rugs on the heated surface.
Prefer thin rugs suitable for underfloor heating.

result.distanceContext: At least {{target}} cm is recommended so air can flow in freely from below. Under 5 cm the air intake is effectively cut off.

notes.sensorAndCold: The room climate check measured this room below its comfort range – together with the enclosed sensor that forms a familiar pattern: the sensor reads trapped heat, shuts off too early, the room stays cool and gets turned up by hand. Freeing the sensor helps more here than any change at the thermostat.
notes.heatPump: Your profile includes a heat pump. Every blocked heat surface has to be compensated by a higher flow temperature – and with a heat pump that immediately costs efficiency. Clearing the obstruction is worth more here than with a condensing boiler.

result.coverContext: The system is sized for the whole floor. Whatever is covered has to be made up by the rest at a higher flow temperature – noticeable from about {{target}} % onwards.
result.mechanismUnderfloor: The heat is not lost – the heating surface sits inside the building envelope. It costs you in two ways: the system is sized for the whole floor, so if part of it drops out, the rest has to deliver the same output at a higher flow temperature – and every degree of flow temperature costs, especially with a heat pump. On top of that, a covered room thermostat measures the trapped heat instead of the room and controls to the wrong value.

base_load.title: Base-load check
base_load.short: Measure how much power your home draws around the clock.

intro.lead: Even with nothing actively running, your home draws power continuously – standby, fridges, router & co. This check reveals that base load.
intro.imageAlt: Illustration: person reading the base load on the electricity meter
steps: Switch off devices in active use – but do not unplug them
Record the meter reading – photograph it or type it in
Read it again later – ideally the next morning
intro.hint: Tip: measuring overnight is the most accurate – nothing you actively use is running then.
details: Even when nothing is actively running, your home draws power continuously – standby, refrigeration, router and so on.

Important: only switch devices off, do not unplug them. Standby draw should be part of the measurement – it is exactly what you want to get rid of later. Always-on devices like the fridge and router stay on anyway.
If your meter shows power directly in watts, you can simply read it off. Otherwise you record the meter reading twice – the app works out the power from the gap.
You do not have to wait between readings: record the value in the evening and read it again the next morning. Overnight also averages out the fridge's cycling.
Measure again later – once you have got rid of always-on consumers. The app will then show you how much you actually saved.

modeHint.instant: Modern meters show current power directly in watts – just read it off.
modeHint.readings: Works with any meter: record the reading, read it again later. No waiting at the meter.

run.instantNote: A snapshot: if the fridge compressor happens to be running, the value comes out much higher. Two readings average that out.
run.resolutionTitle: What is the last digit your meter shows?
run.resolutionHint: The coarser the display, the longer the gap between readings has to be. Recommended: {{duration}}.
run.firstHint: Switch off devices in active use, leave always-on ones like the fridge and router running. Best done in the evening before bed.
run.ready: Ready – you can take the second reading now.
run.waitHint: About {{duration}} left. You can close the app.

quality.fair: Usable, accurate to ±{{pct}}. A longer gap would make the number more reliable.
quality.tooEarly: Too early: your meter only resolves {{resolution}} kWh and has barely moved. Read it again later.

capture.decimalHint: Include the decimal – it is what this measurement depends on.
capture.tooLow: Must be higher than the first reading – meters only count up.
capture.hintFirst: Enter the reading your electricity meter shows right now.
capture.hintSecond: Enter the reading your electricity meter shows right now.

change.title: Before / after
change.down: From {{before}} W to {{after}} W – {{delta}} W less (±{{tolerance}} W). That is around €{{eur}} a year, measured rather than estimated.
change.up: From {{before}} W to {{after}} W – {{delta}} W more (±{{tolerance}} W). A new always-on device?
change.none: From {{before}} W to {{after}} W. The difference is below the measurement accuracy of ±{{tolerance}} W, so it cannot be confirmed.

summary.good: Your base load is low – barely any unnecessary continuous draw here.
summary.medium: Solid base load with a little room to improve.
summary.elevated: Your base load is elevated – worth checking the always-on consumers.
summary.high: High base load – a lot of power is drawn continuously. You should track down the causes.

result.note: Orientation values – base load depends on household size and appliances. This check does not count towards savings itself; the follow-up checks quantify the actual savings.

share.title: Share of your electricity use
share.text: That much of your yearly {{total}} kWh goes to devices running around the clock – even when you are not using anything.
share.basisFullYear: Based on twelve months of your readings.
share.basisProjected: Based on {{days}} days of readings, projected to a year.
share.missing: Add your meter readings in Monitoring – then you will see how much of your electricity bill the base load accounts for.
share.ratedByShare: The rating above refers to this share.

implausible.title: Check the measurement
implausible.text: The base load exceeds your entire yearly consumption – that cannot be right. Devices in active use were probably still running during the measurement. Best to measure again at night.

result.funnelText: Use the standby check to track down the biggest continuous consumers and see what can be switched off.

lighting.title: LED check
lighting.short: One walk through your home to find where switching to LED pays off.

run.lead: An old incandescent or halogen bulb uses about six times the power of an LED at the same brightness. Switching usually pays off quickly – even if the old bulb still works.
run.helpButton: How do I spot an LED?
helpItems: If the bulb gets hot after a minute, it is not an LED.
If it is at full brightness instantly, it is an LED.
If it takes a few seconds to brighten, it is an old energy-saving lamp – worth replacing too.
A visible filament means incandescent or halogen.
run.roomsHint: Is there at least one bulb in this room that is not an LED?

result.summary_one: One room still has old bulbs – start {{room}}.
result.summary_other: {{count}} rooms still have old bulbs – start {{room}}.
result.worthButton: What to look for when buying
result.worth: Mind the right socket (E27, E14, GU10) and warm-white light (2700 K). Lumens replace watts: 60 W is about 800 lm, 40 W about 470 lm.
result.doneSummary_one: The room you checked is already switched over.
result.doneSummary_other: All {{count}} rooms you checked are already switched over.
result.doneTip: Keep choosing warm-white LEDs when you buy replacements.

summary.good: All rooms checked have already been switched to LED.
summary.medium: A few rarely used rooms still have old lamps – those are the next ones worth swapping.
summary.elevated: Several rooms still have old lamps, some of them in daily use. Swapping those pays off quickly.
summary.high: Many heavily used rooms still have old lamps – this is the largest and most quickly realised saving.

remeasure.title: Time to measure again
remeasure.text: You did the {{check}} {{days}} days ago. Measure the base load again – then you will see in black and white what your changes achieved.

completed.subtitle: Your household profile has been saved.

guide.title: What you need in order to measure
guide.intro: Many checks run without buying anything at all. Here is what the others need a device for – and which kind will do.
guide.unusedNoteGeneric: No check currently reads this value.

unusedNote.co2_sensor: No check currently reads the CO₂ value. It is still the most honest indicator of when to air a room – the basics are in the knowledge section.

temperature_sensor.room_thermometer: The standard case for the room climate check. Analogue or digital makes no difference.
temperature_sensor.room_thermostat: Often shows the actual temperature. Fine as long as it does not sit right above the radiator or in the sun.
temperature_sensor.mercury_thermometer: Accurate, but off the market since 2009. If one breaks, it belongs in hazardous waste, not the bin.
temperature_sensor.infrared_surface: Measures surfaces, not room air – good for cold walls, unsuitable for the room climate check.
temperature_sensor.digital_thermometer: With a wireless probe and memory it is handy when you measure several rooms in a row.

humidity_sensor.analog_hygrometer: Cheap, but drifts over the years. Good enough for a rough reading.
humidity_sensor.digital_hygrometer: The straightforward standard for the humidity step of the room climate check.
humidity_sensor.thermo_hygrometer: Temperature and humidity in one device – covers the room climate check on its own.
humidity_sensor.data_logger: Records over days and so catches the humidity peaks after showering or cooking that a single reading misses.
humidity_sensor.smart_sensor: A sensor from your smart home system; the readings are usually in the manufacturer's app.

distance_meter.folding_rule: Perfectly sufficient – what is measured are centimetres, not millimetres.
distance_meter.ruler: Often easier than a folding rule in the narrow gap behind a radiator.
distance_meter.tape_measure: Useful where you cannot reach straight on, because it bends around corners.
distance_meter.laser_distance: Fast and one-handed; below roughly 20 cm often less accurate than a folding rule.
distance_meter.ultrasonic: Measures across an area rather than a point – behind furniture it is easily off.

power_meter.plug_meter: The device for the standby check: plug it between socket and appliance, read the watts. It costs a few euros, and many consumer advice centres and utilities lend one for free.
power_meter.clamp_meter: Measures at the cable without cutting it – needlessly elaborate for the standby check.
power_meter.multimeter: Can measure current, but needs an opened circuit to do so. Not meant for the standby check.
power_meter.electricity_meter: The meter in your building – you need it for the base load check. You can photograph it and the app reads the value.

co2_sensor.portable_monitor: Portable, so suited to comparing several rooms.
co2_sensor.stationary_monitor: Stays in one place and usually records the course of the day.
co2_sensor.traffic_light: Shows green/amber/red instead of a ppm value – meant as a reminder to air the room.
co2_sensor.smart_sensor: A CO₂ sensor from your smart home system; readings are in the manufacturer's app.

tips.title: Recommendations
tips.subtitle: Concrete steps for your home – no tradesperson needed, easiest first.
tips.empty: Run a few measurements first – matching tips will appear here.

standby.title: Switch off standby
standby.reason: Biggest standby item: $t(measurements.standby.deviceTypes.{{deviceType}}) at {{watts}} W. Plug those devices into a switched power strip and turn them all off with one flick.

standby_named.title: Switch off standby
standby_named.reason: Biggest standby item: {{deviceName}} at {{watts}} W. Plug those devices into a switched power strip and turn them all off with one flick.

showerhead.title: Fit a low-flow showerhead
showerhead.reason: Your showerhead delivers {{flow}} L/min. A low-flow head (~8 L/min) screws onto the hose by hand – no tools, same shower feel.

lighting.title: Switch to LED
lighting.reason_one: One room still has old bulbs. A replacement LED costs about 3 € and earns that back in the first year.
lighting.reason_other: {{count}} rooms still have old bulbs. Start where the light is on longest – a replacement LED costs about 3 € and earns that back in the first year.

hot_water_wait.title: Catch the run-off water
hot_water_wait.reason: It takes {{seconds}} s for hot water to arrive – about {{liters}} L runs off unused every time, roughly {{litersPerYear}} L over a year. Put a watering can or bucket underneath: for plants, cleaning or the toilet.

hot_water_wait_unknown.title: Catch the run-off water
hot_water_wait_unknown.reason: It takes {{seconds}} s for hot water to arrive – cold water runs off unused during that time. The exact amount hasn't been measured for this tap yet. Put a watering can or bucket underneath: for plants, cleaning or the toilet.

fridge.title: Turn the fridge up
fridge.reason: {{temp}} °C is colder than needed. Turn the dial down one notch – 7 °C is plenty, andeach degree warmer saves around 6 % electricity.

fridge_warm.title: Turn the fridge down
fridge_warm.reason: {{temp}} °C is too warm for safe storage. Turn the dial up one notch until you reach 5–7 °C.

freezer.title: Defrost the freezer
freezer.reason: A layer of ice drives consumption up. Switch it off, open the door, lay out towels – it costs you one afternoon.

room_temperature.title: Lower the room temperature
room_temperature.reason: {{room}} is at {{temp}} °C. Turn the thermostat back half a notch: one degree less saves around 6 % heating energy and is barely noticeable.
room_temperature.reasonNoRoom: It's {{temp}} °C here. Turn the thermostat back half a notch: one degree less saves around 6 % heating energy and is barely noticeable.

room_cold.title: Don't let the room go cold
room_cold.reason: {{room}} is at {{temp}} °C. Permanently cool rooms get damp and mould-prone. Set the thermostat to a low constant level instead of switching off and reheating later.
room_cold.reasonNoRoom: It's only {{temp}} °C here. Permanently cool rooms get damp and mould-prone. Set the thermostat to a low constant level instead of switching off and reheating later.

humidity_high.title: Air out against damp
humidity_high.reason: {{room}} is at {{humidity}} % humidity – too high. Air out two to three times a day for 5 minutes with the window wide open, instead of leaving it tilted.
humidity_high.reasonNoRoom: Humidity is at {{humidity}} % – too high. Air out two to three times a day for 5 minutes with the window wide open, instead of leaving it tilted.

humidity_low.title: The air is too dry
humidity_low.reason: {{room}} is at {{humidity}} % humidity – very dry, which irritates the airways. Shorter airing and not overheating usually does it.
humidity_low.reasonNoRoom: Humidity is at {{humidity}} % – very dry, which irritates the airways. Shorter airing and not overheating usually does it.

draft.title: Seal the draught
draft.reason: {{room}}: there's a noticeable draught at a window or door. Self-adhesive sealing tape from the hardware store presses straight into the frame – peel, press, done.
draft.reasonNoRoom: There's a noticeable draught at a window or door. Self-adhesive sealing tape from the hardware store presses straight into the frame – peel, press, done.

furniture_spacing.title: Clear the radiator
furniture_spacing.reason: Furniture or curtains sit too close and trap the heat. Move them back a little – from about 30 cm the warmth reaches the room.

base_load.title: Track down constant draws
base_load.reason: Your base load is {{watts}} W – even with nothing running on purpose. The standby check shows you device by device where it comes from.

consumption_up.title: More $t(monitoring.energyTypes.{{carrier}}) than last year
consumption_up.reason: Your meter readings show {{percent}} % more consumption than the same period last year – about {{amount}} {{unit}} extra. That is measured, not estimated. Find the cause before it adds up over another year.

old_boiler.title: Consider replacing the boiler
old_boiler.reason: Your boiler is about {{years}} years old. Replacing it is the single biggest lever in your home – such measures usually qualify for public funding, which is worth checking.

pv_self_consumption.title: Move big loads into the sunny hours
pv_self_consumption.reason: Electricity you use yourself is worth what you would otherwise pay for it – electricity you feed in only earns the feed-in tariff, which is considerably lower. Use the delayed start on your dishwasher and washing machine to run them around midday, charge the car and your batteries then, and heat hot water at noon. This is not about using less, it is about shifting when.

pv_planned_base_load.title: Before sizing the system: measure your base load
pv_planned_base_load.reason: How large your system should sensibly be depends less on the roof than on how much electricity can stay in the house at all. Base load is the most useful number for that – measure it before you compare quotes. The check takes a few minutes and runs overnight.
